list.listitem: Hirsutism is excessive male pattern hair growth in females. Most often it is due to polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) but may be idiopathic. B
Serum androgen assays (beginning with plasma free testosterone) are the mainstay of diagnosis. C
Exercise and diet to promote weight loss are first-line treatment, particularly in patients with PCOS. B
Along with treatment of the underlying disorder (if any), oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), antiandrogen drugs, and laser therapy may be effective. B

background.definition: Hirsutism is excessive male pattern hair growth, typically thick (terminal) hair growth on the face and other body regions. Hirsutism may be the initial, and possibly only, sign of an underlying androgen disorder, the cutaneous manifestations of which may also include acne and male pattern balding (androgenic alopecia). In contrast to hirsutism, hypertrichosis is excessive hair growth in either sex, which can be on the entire body surface and is not due to endocrine disorders.

list.listitem: Hirsutism affects approximately 5% to 10% of females of reproductive age.
Estimates of the prevalence of PCOS in the general population have ranged from 2% to 20%.
Changes in appearance like obesity and hirsutism reduce physical dimensions of quality of life and have significant psychosocial impact.
See Differential Diagnosis table.
The most common type of hirsutism is caused by PCOS.
The second most common type is idiopathic hirsutism.
In a small minority of cases hirsutism is the result of a serious adrenal or ovarian disorder, such as a tumor, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), or severe insulin resistance syndromes.
Androgenic drugs include danazol and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs).
Cushing's syndrome is associated with both hypertrichosis of hair and hirsutism.
Patients with no identifiable cause and normal serum androgen levels are labeled as having idiopathic hirsutism.
Hirsutism is caused by increased androgen production (testosterone and androstenediones) by the ovaries, adrenal glands, or both.
See chapter on PCOS for information on pathophysiology of that condition.
A physical examination using the modified Ferriman–Gallwey (FG) score for the initial diagnosis of hirsutism may warrant further laboratory tests. C
The single most sensitive test in the diagnosis of hirsutism is plasma free testosterone. C
Ultrasound can be used for confirming classical PCOS cases but is not very specific. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, menstrual disturbances, obesity, acne vulgaris
No identifiable cause and normal serum androgen levels
21-Hydroxylase deficiency with salt wasting, hyperkalemia, virilization—classic CAH
Rapidly progressive hirsutism with elevated serum testosterone levels
Rapidly progressive hirsutism with elevated serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) levels
Hyperinsulinemia and increased serum free testosterone levels

list.listitem: Hirsutism can be an early sign of a virilizing adrenal carcinoma or adenoma, as well as of adrenal hyperplasia and ovarian disorders. Rapid progression of hirsutism suggests neoplasm; this cannot be excluded on the basis of the history or physical examination.
Obtain a menstrual history to determine ovulation status and take a history of any medication use that could cause androgen excess.
Classic CAH can present as genital ambiguity in newborn, whereas nonclassic CAH presents in adolescence.
History of onset and progression of hirsutism, family history (points toward PCOS/CAH), weight gain, and medication history is vital.

The degree of hirsutism can be assessed during physical examination by the modified FG score, which records the distribution and severity of excess body hair. Hair growth is rated from 0 (no growth of terminal hair) to 4 (complete and heavy cover) in 9 locations. The 9 locations measured are the upper lip, chin, chest, upper back, lower back, upper abdomen, lower abdomen, the upper arms, and the thighs. A score of 3 and above indicates abnormal hair growth.
On physical examination, also look for signs of virilization (eg, acne, clitoromegaly, deep voice), and calculate body mass index to assess for obesity and guide weight loss counseling.

Laboratory testing is not always required but may be done for confirmation of androgen excess and etiology. A practice guideline recommends testing for elevated androgen levels in women with moderate to severe hirsutism, and when hirsutism is sudden in onset, associated with obesity, menstrual dysfunction, obesity, or clitoromegaly, or is rapidly progressive.
Laboratory testing should begin with plasma free testosterone, since it is the single most sensitive test for detection of androgen excess.

In case of rapid hirsutism and signs of virilization, ovarian/adrenal tumor must be suspected. Elevated levels of serum DHEAS are consistent with adrenal hyperandrogenism (adrenal tumor). In such cases, order imaging (CT scan/ultrasound [US]) to detect tumors.
An overnight dexamethasone suppression test can be done if Cushing's syndrome is suspected (central obesity, moon facies, amenorrhoea, etc).
Serum 17 OH progesterone levels above 200 ng/dl suggest CAH (infertility, virilization, etc).

Impaired glucose tolerance test and type 2 diabetes mellitus incidence is increased in PCOS; hence an oral glucose tolerance test is recommended in obese patients. Also an increased luteinizing hormone/follicle stimulating hormone ratio can be found in PCOS.
PCOS on pelvic US is found in only 65% adolescents and 75% adult women; hence it is not required for the diagnosis.
A simple questionnaire completed by patients prior to meeting the physician can assist in the diagnosis of PCOS. However, it has only been validated in a referral setting.
Consider evaluating for PCOS in women with hirsutism.
Slowly progressive hirsutism with anovulation of peripubertal onset usually requires an evaluation to rule out other endocrinopathies (adult-onset CAH, hyperprolactinemia, and Cushing's syndrome).
Virilization or severe rapidly progressive hirsutism requires immediate investigation to rule out a possible virilizing tumor.
Regular exercise and a healthy diet to promote weight loss in overweight women are first-line therapy, especially for patients with PCOS. B
Based on low-certainty evidence, effective medications include oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), spironolactone 100 mg daily, and flutamide 250 mg twice daily. B
Laser epilation techniques may be effective for short-term hair removal. B
Pharmacologic treatment should be considered after 6 to 9 months of weight loss and lifestyle interventions; it revolves around suppression of androgen production and androgen receptor blockade.

Based on low quality evidence, a Cochrane review fconcluded thatal contraceptive pills (OCPs), spironolactone 100 mg daily, and flutamide 250 mg twice daily effwere ective for hirsutism. Finasteride and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues showed inconsistent outcomes, while metformin may be ineffective, again based on low quality evidence.

An earlier systematic review of 28 RCTs found a significant reduction in hirsutism with flutamide, spironolactone, cyproterone acetate combined with an OCP, thiazolidinediones, OCPs, finasteride, and metformin.

Antiandrogens are the first-line drugs in severe cases of hirsutism. Flutamide is a potent nonsteroidal antiandrogen used for hirsutism. A 30% to 50% reduction in FG score is noted after treatment of 9 months with antiandrogens. However, caution with the use of flutamide is recommended by the FDA due to reports of hospitalization and rarely death due to flutamide-associated hepatic failure.

Finasteride is a 5-alfa reductase inhibitor used for hirsutism but is not as potent as antiandrogens. Both finasteride and flutamide are not Food and Drug Administration approved for treatment of hirsutism.
Spironolactone treatment for 6 months is associated with a statistically significant subjective improvement in hair growth and FG scores and is considered superior to finasteride.

One study showed that the effectiveness of spironolactone (100 mg/d), flutamide (250 mg/d), and finasteride (5 mg/d) are similar when compared at 6 months. However, a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs found that antiandrogens were more effective than metformin but equally effective as OCPs. Combination therapy (finasteride or spironolactone with OCPs and flutamide with metformin) was more effective than OCPs or metformin alone.
A Cochrane review found that, among adult women with PCOS, metformin and OCPs are effective for hirsutism. Statins have uncertain effectiveness for hirsutism.

Other treatment options can be tailored to specific etiologies of hirsutism: Glucocorticoids are used in patients with excess adrenal androgens (DHEAS) due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Metformin may normalize menses and decrease hirsutism score in teenagers with oligomenorrhea and PCOS.
Oral contraception is considered first line in hyperandrogenism for those interested in birth control and is similarly effective to metformin.
Eflornithine topical cream can be used indefinitely to prevent regrowth of facial hair.

A network meta-analysis of 32 randomized trials concluded there was strongest evidence for efficacy of combination estrogen-progestin OCPs, anti-androgens (primarily for women who are using long-acting contraception or who have been sterilized) and metformin. All OCPs appeared to be similarly effective.

Epilation with laser devices (alexandrite, diode, yttrium aluminum garnet, and ruby lasers) and intense pulsed light (IPL) are commonly used for temporary hair removal. Paradoxical hypertrichosis and terminal hair change is a complication of IPL photoepilation; in one study occurring in 5% of patients. Alexandrite laser, in particular, has been studied and found to be safe and effective.

A systematic review of 6 RCTs involving 423 patients evaluating laser and light-based therapies found low-certainty evidence for their effectiveness in treating hirsutism in women with PCOS, but cautions physicians regarding the uncertainty of their efficacy and safety amongs patients of color.
While ovarian surgery can decrease androgen levels, its role in treating hirsutism per se is still not clear.
Surgical removal of tumor is needed in cases of ovarian or adrenal tumors.
There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of acupuncture or Chinese herbal medicine for the treatment of hirsutism among women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).
Soybean extracts have shown to reduce hair growth and decrease hair shaft dimensions.

Mechanical hair removal and lifestyle changes are the nonpharmacologic ways to treat hirsutism and to hasten therapeutic response. These should be attempted first and as adjuncts to medication, since medication alone takes at least 6 to 9 months to show significant improvement.

A balanced diet and adequate exercise can help control weight, which may diminish or prevent hirsutism related to obesity. Weight loss improves practically every parameter of PCOS-related hirsutism. All the parameters show noticeable improvement with as little as 5% weight reduction.
Long-term medical therapy with antiandrogens and/or OCPs is advisable to prevent relapse. C
